items.scene: A student from a rival school answers a question in class. Before hearing the full answer, several classmates assume it is probably disrespectful.
items.question: What best explains the classmates' reaction?
options: They are judging the student through out-group bias and a group label.
They think the student has formal authority in the class.
They are reacting to a broken promise from that student.
They want to keep private information from the student.
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a direct identity-based interpretation: the same behavior is read negatively because of out-group membership.

items.scene: A manager gives the same blunt feedback to two workers. One worker says the comment sounds harsh but fair because the manager is their boss.
items.question: What is the main driver of the worker's interpretation?
options: A stereotype about a rival club
A need to protect a secret
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a close near-miss: the cue is power and role, not group identity.

items.scene: A neighbor says a man is unreliable because he missed two earlier meetings after promising to come.
items.question: Why is he being judged as unreliable?
options: Because he belongs to an out-group
Because of a stereotype about his neighborhood club
Because of his past behavior and broken promise
Because he has a lower-status job
items.why_this_case_matters: This is a boundary case: the judgment is based on history, not identity-bound inference.

items.scene: A teacher does not share a student's personal note with the class, even though the student is from the rival debate team.
items.question: What is the main issue here?
items.why_this_case_matters: This includes a group label, but the real issue is whether information may be disclosed, not identity-based interpretation.
